title: Adam and Christ (Romans 5:12–21)
hook: where sin increased, grace abounded all the more

segments.voice: Yesterday, peace with God, and the chain from tribulation to hope. Your line was hope does not disappoint. Did you tell someone about a hard season that grew you? Day three hundred seventeen.

Some things you inherit without asking. Your grandmother's nose. Your family's way of going quiet when things get tense. A house, or a debt. You didn't choose any of it, and it shapes you anyway. Paul, in the second half of Romans chapter five, steps way back from Rome and from his own day, all the way back to the garden in Genesis. He's thinking about the whole human family and what it has inherited. And he sets two figures side by side, like two ends of a seesaw: the first man, and one more. Today is those two names.
screen: `THINGS YOU INHERIT WITHOUT ASKING.` → `BACK TO THE GARDEN.` → `TWO FIGURES, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: Paul begins, in the King James Bible: "Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned." One man, Adam, opened a door, and sin and death came through it into the whole human story. Then Paul sets up the other end of the seesaw: "For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous." Adam and Christ. One disobeyed, one obeyed. One brought death, one brings life. But here's what Paul keeps insisting: it isn't an even seesaw. Again and again he says much more. The gift is not like the fall. Then comes the line of the day: "But where sin abounded, grace did much more abound." Paul is so eager here he reaches for a rare super-word in Greek: grace super-abounded, over-overflowed. However big the mess gets, grace is bigger. Now, Christians understand the Adam side differently, so here's who says what. In the West, following Augustine, Catholics and most Protestants speak of original sin: every person is born sharing in Adam's fallen state, even in some sense his guilt. Orthodox Christians usually speak of ancestral sin: we inherit mortality and a wounded nature, but not Adam's personal guilt. Part of that difference goes back to how one small phrase in this passage was translated into Latin. What every church agrees on is Paul's direction of travel. The chapter doesn't end with Adam. It ends with grace reigning, through Jesus Christ.
screen: `BY ONE MAN SIN ENTERED.` · `BY THE OBEDIENCE OF ONE.` · `NOT AN EVEN SEESAW: MUCH MORE.` · `ORIGINAL SIN, ANCESTRAL SIN.` · then, large: `GRACE DID MUCH MORE ABOUND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice grace bigger than a mistake. Settle, and breathe. Think of a mistake, yours or someone else's, that turned out to be smaller than what came after it. A fight that ended in a better friendship. A wrong turn that led somewhere good. Someone who forgave you more than you expected. Don't explain it away. Just let yourself see that the mistake didn't get the last word. Breathe out, and let that sink in. If you pray, you can thank God for that grace, by name. The bell holds the time.
Adam and Christ. The first man and the one who obeyed, set side by side by Paul, with grace always the heavier side.
Your line: grace abounds. Today, when a mistake, yours or someone else's, looks like it's going to have the last word, say those two words under your breath. Day three hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Christians read Romans 5 when they teach about sin and salvation, and in the Easter Vigil's ancient hymn, the Exsultet, many churches sing of Adam's fall and of the grace that came after it.

fork.setup: you're Paul. you've just said sin and death came into the world through one man. how do you describe what Christ brings?
options: exactly equal: one cancels out the other.
much more: where sin abounded, grace abounded more.
smaller: enough for some, not for all.

original.note: Greek: grace, favor, a gift freely given. the root of the word Eucharist, thanksgiving.

trapdoor: what you thought: Adam and Christ is a history lesson about two people.
what it means: Paul sets them side by side: one opened the door to sin and death, one to life, and grace is always the heavier side.
what a scholar hears: Paul's Greek eph' hō in 5:12 likely means because all sinned, but the Latin Bible read in whom all sinned, which shaped Augustine's teaching on original sin.

notes: 'Super-abounded' renders hyperperisseuō (Romans 5:20); the verb is rare (also 2 Corinthians 7:4). The script says Paul 'reaches for a rare super-word'; confirm.
Original sin vs. ancestral sin: compressed summary. Confirm fairness to Catholic, Protestant (Reformed/Lutheran vs. others) and Orthodox teaching, including the phrase 'even in some sense his guilt'.
Eph' hō (Romans 5:12): the Old Latin/Vulgate 'in quo omnes peccaverunt' and its influence on Augustine is standard scholarship; confirm the trapdoor wording.
howItsDone: the Exsultet ('O happy fault') is sung at the Easter Vigil in Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran churches; confirm the general phrasing 'many churches'.
